name: Infinity embedding and reranking server
notable_features: The only engine in this slice that spans the whole retrieval stack in one process: text embeddings, reranking, CLIP, CLAP and ColPali, multi-model at once, with the orchestration done by Infinity itself.

Three interchangeable inference backends behind one API - PyTorch, Optimum (ONNX/TensorRT) and CTranslate2 - selected per model rather than per deployment. That is a genuine operational advantage: the same serving contract across three kernel stacks.
FlashAttention is used to get the most out of NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, CPU, AWS INF2 and Apple MPS - the same compute-bound assumption as TEI, stated as an explicit design choice.

Dynamic batching plus tokenization dedicated to worker threads, so tokenization does not serialize behind the forward pass. For encoders this matters more than it looks: tokenization is a real fraction of a 100M-param encoder's wall clock, unlike a 70B decode where it is noise.
OpenAPI aligned to OpenAI's embeddings specification, so existing SDKs work; FastAPI-based; CLI v2 can launch everything via environment variable or argument.
Adopters listed in the README span Baseten, RunPod, TrueFoundry, Vast.ai, SAP AI Core, BentoML, Hugging Face chat-ui and others - real production use, not a demo.
hardware_caveats: Name collision that matters for research: infiniflow/infinity is a different, unrelated project - an AI-native vector DATABASE with hybrid search, 4733 stars. It does not run embedding inference by default; it is a retrieval store. The serving engine here is michaelfeil/infinity. Do not conflate the two when grepping citations.
Apple MPS is supported but is the least-documented accelerator path in the README; the AWS INF2 path is mentioned alongside CUDA/ROCm/CPU rather than detailed.

Because the backend (PyTorch / ONNX-TensorRT / CTranslate2) is a per-model choice, peak throughput is not uniform across models in one deployment - a model served on the ONNX path and one on the PyTorch path in the same process will not behave comparably under load.
Last push 2026-03-24, so the project is active but no longer moving at the pace of TEI; dependency churn in the Optimum/CTranslate2 chain is the operational risk to watch.
best_for: One server for embeddings AND reranking, when you would otherwise run two deployments and reconcile their batching policies.
Multi-model and multi-modal retrieval: CLIP/CLAP/ColPali alongside text encoders, with Infinity doing the orchestration.
Apple Silicon and AWS Inferentia2 deployments - unusual accelerator coverage for a retrieval-serving engine.
Teams that want per-model backend selection (ONNX/TensorRT for some models, PyTorch+FlashAttention for others) behind one HTTP contract.
Anyone who wants a ColPali-style multimodal retriever without building one.
avoid_for: Expecting the vendor-grade operational polish of TEI - smaller project, slower cadence, thinner documentation of failure modes.
Deployments where every model must run on one backend for reproducible benchmarking.
CUDA compute capabilities below what FlashAttention supports, or ROCm configurations the README does not cover.
notes: COMPUTE-BOUND at batch 1 for a BERT-size encoder, same mechanism as TEI and for the same reason: a bidirectional encoder runs full attention over all input tokens in a single pass with no KV cache and no autoregressive streaming, so the cost is dense GEMM plus a full (non-causal, hence unhalved) attention matrix rather than a bandwidth-bound weight-streaming loop. What makes Infinity's README unusually explicit about this is that it names FlashAttention as the throughput lever across five accelerator families - a compute-efficiency story, not a bandwidth story. Hardware selection consequence: prefer FLOPS and cache-friendly capacity over HBM bandwidth. An encoder of 100-500M params in fp16 is 200 MB - 1 GB of weights, which fits in the L2 of a server GPU or even in unified memory on Apple Silicon; the interesting question is not 'does the model fit' but 'how many FLOPs can you throw at it', which in practice means: fill --max-batch-tokens / the dynamic-batch queue with short passages and let FlashAttention amortize. Contrast with an LLM decode part on the same machine, where the correct instinct is the opposite - buy bandwidth, accept low occupancy. For reranking the compute-boundedness is even stronger and needs stating explicitly, because it is the single most under-budgeted line item in RAG pipelines: a cross-encoder must encode the concatenated query+passage for EVERY candidate, so reranking a top-k of k costs roughly k times a full-length forward pass with zero opportunity for caching or early exit. bge-reranker-v2-m3 class models at 512-1024 tokens make a top-100 rerank one to two orders of magnitude more FLOPs than embedding the entire candidate set was. Architectures served: because it wraps three general-purpose backends rather than a bespoke encoder implementation, the coverage is 'any model the HuggingFace text-embeddings tag carries' - BERT/XLM-RoBERTa/GTE/E5-class encoders, Qwen/Mistral/Gemma decoder-based embedders, CLIP and ColPali. Can serve: dense bi-encoders, cross-encoders, CLIP-family and late-interaction-multimodal. Cannot serve well: models needing token-wise output for ColBERT MaxSim in a single-vector store, and quantized formats outside what ONNX/CTranslate2 can express. confidence 0.82: the backend and accelerator claims are quoted from the README, but the README gives no benchmark table with methodology, so throughput claims are unquantified here.
